British rule over the Indian subcontinent, from the Battle of Plassey in 1757 to independence and partition in 1947. For its first century it was the rule of a trading company; from 1858 it was the rule of the British Crown, known as the Raj.

Company rule (1757 to 1858). The East India Company took Bengal, then by war and treaty most of India. It ruled some lands directly and bound hundreds of Indian princes to it by treaty. The rebellion of 1857, begun by the Company's own Indian soldiers, spread across the north and was put down with great brutality.

Crown rule (1858 to 1947). Parliament took over. A viceroy ruled British India, about three fifths of the land, while some 560 princely states kept their rulers under British supervision. Queen Victoria became Empress of India in 1877. The capital moved from Calcutta to New Delhi in 1911.

What it brought and took:

  • Railways, telegraphs, irrigation canals, ports and an English-educated class.
  • Indian textile industries lost ground to British factory cloth, and much of India's revenue went to pay for the government, the army and debts in Britain.
  • Great famines killed millions, in the 1870s, the 1890s and in the Bengal famine of 1943.
  • Millions of Indian soldiers fought in the world wars.

The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, grew into a mass movement under Gandhi from about 1920, using non-violent non-cooperation. After the Second World War, Britain left. In August 1947 British India was split into India and Pakistan in the Partition, amid mass killing and the flight of millions.
